title: Reading a log scale chart
objectives: Read a price chart on a log axis, where equal steps mean equal percentage moves
Find the price halfway between two gridlines of a log scale
Read a continuous growth rate from the gradient of a straight line on a log scale

screens.title: Reading a log scale chart
screens.prose: Long price charts are often drawn on a log scale. We will see what that scale measures, and how to read it.
A share grows by the same 15% every year for 20 years. On an ordinary price axis the last few years look explosive.

state.caption: A share growing 15% a year for 20 years, on an ordinary price axis

screens.question: In percentage terms, which five years grew faster: years 0 to 5, or years 15 to 20?

options.why: You read the size of the rise in pounds. £82.30 is a bigger rise than £10.11, but each is a doubling of where it started.
You may have felt the early years were the real growth. Both stretches multiply the price by 2.01.

hints.text: Divide the end price by the start price for each stretch.
Compare £20.11 over £10.00 with £163.67 over £81.37.
$\tfrac{20.11}{10.00} = 2.01$ and $\tfrac{163.67}{81.37} = 2.01$. Same ratio, same percentage.

feedback.correct: Both stretches multiply the price by 2.01.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the ratios, not the pound amounts.

byKey.late: You compared pounds. The later rise is bigger in pounds only because the price was bigger to start with.

explain.text: Each five years multiplies the price by $1.15^5 = 2.01$. The ordinary axis shows pounds, so later moves look huge. We want a chart where equal percentage moves look equal.

screens.prose: Here is the same share with ln of the price on the vertical axis. The dashed lines mark prices. Slide the five-year window along.
screens.question: As you slide the window, what happens to the height of the solid rise?

options.why: That was true of the ordinary chart. Here the height is ln of the price, and each rise is 0.70 wherever it sits.
Look at the rise at year 0 and at year 15: both span the same height.

hints.text: Compare the rise at the start with the rise at year 15.

feedback.correct: Every five-year rise has the same height.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Watch the solid vertical segment as you slide.

explain.text: Each rise is $\ln 2.01 = 0.70$, because each five years multiplies the price by 2.01. The price path is a straight line. The dashed price lines are equally spaced too: each is a doubling of the one below.

screens.prose: A chart whose height is ln of the price, with the gridlines labelled in prices, is a **log scale chart**. Equal heights mean equal ratios. l7's base-10 log draws the same picture; only the units of height change.

state.caption: M sits exactly halfway up between the two gridlines

screens.question: What price does M mark?

widget.label: Price at M
widget.accept: £100.00: two equal steps, each a doubling, from £50.00 to £200.00.

hints.text: £50.00 to £200.00 multiplies by 4. What multiplies twice to make 4?
M splits the climb into two equal heights, so two equal ratios.
Each half multiplies by 2: £50.00 to £100.00 to £200.00.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Halfway up means half of the ratio, not half of the pounds.

byKey.mid: You took the midpoint in pounds. On a log scale, halfway up splits the ratio 4 into $2 \times 2$, so M is £100.00.

explain.text: M splits the climb into two equal heights. Equal heights are equal ratios, so each half multiplies by 2. M is £100.00, not £125.00.

screens.prose: On a log scale chart, two shares each rise 50%. Share A goes from £20.00 to £30.00. Share B goes from £100.00 to £150.00.
screens.question: Which rise will be taller on the log scale chart?

options.text: Both rises are the same height

options.why: You compared the pound amounts: £50.00 against £10.00. A log scale measures ratios, and both are 1.5.
You may have expected small prices to stretch out. Both multiply by 1.5, so both rise by $\ln 1.5$.

hints.text: What does each price multiply by?
Both start points are marked.
Both rises multiply by 1.5, so both are $\ln 1.5 = 0.41$ tall.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the ratios of the moves.

explain.text: Both prices multiply by 1.5, so both rise $\ln 1.5 = 0.41$. On a log scale, equal percentage moves are equal heights. A £10 move on a £20 share counts as much as £50 on £100.

screens.prose: Now the gridlines are £100.00 and £200.00, one doubling apart. N sits exactly halfway up between them.

state.caption: N sits exactly halfway up between the two gridlines

screens.question: What price does N mark? Give two decimal places.

hints.text: Two equal steps from £100.00 to £200.00 must each multiply by the same number.
That number, times itself, makes 2.
Each step multiplies by $\sqrt{2} = 1.4142$, so N is £141.42.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Halfway up splits the ratio 2 into two equal factors.

byKey.mid: You took the midpoint in pounds. Halfway up on a log scale is the ratio $\sqrt{2}$ from each end, so £141.42.

explain.text: Each half of the climb multiplies by the same factor, and the two factors make 2. So each is $\sqrt{2} = 1.4142$, and N is £141.42. Check: $141.42 \times 1.4142 = 200$.

screens.prose: Log scale gridlines at £100, £200 and £400 are equally spaced. Drag P up or down until it marks a price of £300.00.
screens.question: Place P at £300.00.

hints.text: The caption shows the price P marks as you drag.
£300.00 lies between the £200 and £400 gridlines.
£300.00 is 1.5 times £200.00, and $\ln 1.5 = 0.41$ out of the step of 0.69. So P sits 58% of the way up.

feedback.correct: £300.00 sits a little above halfway, 58% of the way from £200 to £400.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the caption as you drag.

byKey.halfway: You placed P halfway between £200 and £400, as on a pound axis. Halfway up on a log scale is £282.84; £300.00 sits a little higher.
byKey.P: P is not at £300.00 yet. Watch the caption and stop when it reads close to £300.00.

explain.text: £300.00 is £200.00 times 1.5. That is $\tfrac{\ln 1.5}{\ln 2} = 0.58$ of a doubling step, a little above halfway. The halfway mark is £282.84, not £300.00.

screens.prose: On a log scale chart the height is $\ln P$. A rise of $h$ means the price multiplied by $e^h$, so equal heights are equal percentage moves. Steady growth $P = P_0e^{kt}$ plots as $\ln P = \ln P_0 + kt$: a straight line with gradient $k$.
screens.question: On a log scale chart, a share's line is straight for ten years. What does that tell you?

options.text: It grew by the same percentage each year
It gained the same number of pounds each year
options.why: That is what a straight line means on an ordinary axis. On a log scale, straight means a steady ratio.
A flat line would mean that. A rising straight line means steady percentage growth.

hints.text: On a log scale, what do equal heights stand for?

feedback.correct: A straight line on a log scale is steady percentage growth.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Equal steps up are equal ratios.

explain.text: Equal years give equal rises, and equal rises are equal ratios. So the share grew at a constant rate. The gradient of the line is that continuous rate $k$.

screens.prose: Why does steady growth $P = P_0e^{kt}$ draw a straight line on a log scale? Take ln of the price.
screens.question: Put the steps in order.

lines.text: $\ln P = \ln(P_0e^{kt})$: take ln of both sides
$= \ln P_0 + \ln(e^{kt})$: the log of a product is a sum
A straight line in $t$, with height $\ln P_0$ at $t = 0$ and gradient $k$

hints.text: Begin by taking ln of the growth formula.
Take ln, split the product, undo the $e$, then read off the line.

feedback.correct: $\ln P = \ln P_0 + kt$: intercept $\ln P_0$, gradient $k$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each line rewrites the one above it.

byKey.d3: ln can only undo the $e$ once $\ln(e^{kt})$ stands alone, after the product is split.
byKey.d2: First take ln of both sides.

explain.text: Splitting the product gives $\ln P_0 + \ln(e^{kt})$, and ln undoes $e$ to leave $kt$. So $\ln P$ rises by $k$ every year. The gradient of a log chart is the continuous growth rate.

screens.prose: A backtest's equity is drawn on a log scale. It hugs a straight line from £100,000.00 in 2016 to £400,000.00 in 2026.

state.caption: A backtest's equity curve on a log scale

screens.question: What continuous yearly growth rate does the straight trend show? Give a percentage to two decimal places.

hints.text: The gradient is the rise in $\ln$ equity divided by the years.
The line climbs two doubling gridlines, from £100,000 to £400,000.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the rise in ln equity by 10 years.

byKey.simple: You spread the 300% gain evenly over 10 years. Growth compounds; the gradient of the log chart is $\tfrac{\ln 4}{10}$.
byKey.yearly: That is $4^{0.1} - 1$, the rate paid once a year. The gradient of the chart is the continuous rate.
byKey.log10: You used the base-10 log. The chart's height is ln, so use $\ln 4$.

explain.text: The line climbs $\ln 4 = 1.3863$ in 10 years, a gradient of 0.1386. So the strategy compounded at 13.86% a year, continuously. Two doublings in 10 years is one doubling every 5: $\tfrac{\ln 2}{0.1386} = 5$.

ideas: A log scale chart plots $\ln P$ and labels the heights with prices.
Equal heights are equal ratios, so equal percentage moves look the same size anywhere on the chart.
Steady growth draws a straight line, and its gradient is the continuous growth rate $k$.

formula.name: Log scale
formula.note: A rise of $h$ on the chart means the price multiplied by $e^h$.

summary.trap: A log axis is not evenly spaced in pounds. Halfway between £200 and £400 is £282.84, not £300.

quiz.prose: On a log scale chart, a share rises the same height from 2019 to 2020 as from 2023 to 2024. From 2019 to 2020 it rose 20%.
quiz.question: How much did it rise from 2023 to 2024?

options.text: More than 20%, since the price was higher
options.why: You treated height as pounds. On a log scale equal heights are equal percentages.
Equal heights mean equal ratios, whatever the price level.

feedback.correct: Equal heights are equal percentage moves: 20%.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Equal heights mean equal ratios.

explain.text: A log scale turns ratios into heights. The same height means the same ratio, 1.2, so the same 20% rise.

quiz.prose: Gridlines at £10, £100 and £1,000 are equally spaced on a log scale chart. A point sits exactly halfway up between £10 and £100.
quiz.question: What price does it mark? Give two decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Halfway up splits the ratio 10 into two equal factors.

byKey.mid: You took the midpoint in pounds. Halfway up on a log scale is the ratio $\sqrt{10} = 3.162$ from £10.

explain.text: From £10 to £100 multiplies by 10. Two equal steps each multiply by $\sqrt{10} = 3.162$, so the point is £31.62.

quiz.prose: On a log scale chart a share's straight line runs from £30.00 to £120.00 over 4 years.
quiz.question: What continuous growth rate does it show? Give a percentage to two decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the rise in ln price by the years.

byKey.simple: You spread the 300% gain over 4 years. The gradient of a log chart is $\tfrac{\ln 4}{4}$.
byKey.yearly: That is $4^{1/4} - 1$, the rate paid once a year. The gradient gives the continuous rate.

explain.text: The price multiplies by 4, a rise of $\ln 4 = 1.3863$, over 4 years. The gradient is 0.3466: a continuous rate of 34.66%.

quiz.prose: Two shares are drawn on the same log scale chart. Share A's line is steeper than share B's over the same year.
quiz.question: What must be true?

options.text: A grew by a larger percentage

options.why: A cheap share can be steeper while gaining fewer pounds. Gradient on a log scale is a growth rate.
Height on the chart gives price, but steepness gives growth. A low line can be the steeper one.

feedback.correct: Steeper on a log scale means a faster percentage rate.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Gradient on a log scale is the growth rate.

explain.text: The gradient of $\ln P$ is the continuous growth rate. So the steeper line grew by the larger percentage, whatever the prices.
